Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old man with known asthma presented via telehealth with 3 hours of acute chest tightness, wheeze, and mild exertional shortness of breath following a recent cold and a 1-week lapse in inhalers; managed as an acute asthma exacerbation with SABA/ICS refills, a short oral steroid course, spacer, and safety-netting.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Chest tightness for ~3 hours.
- Symptoms: Mild shortness of breath (not at rest), wheeze, non-productive cough; feels unable to take a full breath at times.
- Recent illness: Had a cold last week (sore throat, runny nose); nasal symptoms improved but cough persists.
- Pattern: Cough slightly worse at night; dyspnea increases with exertion (stairs).
- Chest pain: Denies pain; describes tightness.
- Medication use: Ran out of both inhalers about a week ago and has not used them since.
- Severity/function: Not short of breath at rest; more winded than usual on stairs.
- Pertinent negatives (as stated): No productive sputum.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma since childhood; prior severe exacerbation requiring intubation and hospital stay at ~16–17 years.
- Atopy: Allergic rhinitis/hay fever; dust allergy.
- Childhood eczema; childhood milk protein allergy.

Medications:
- Previously prescribed:
  - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler PRN – ran out ~1 week ago; currently none in possession; dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler – ran out ~1 week ago; currently none in possession; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- To be prescribed today (per plan):
  - Ventolin inhaler – PRN (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Clenil Modulite inhaler – controller to resume when improving (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Oral steroid tablets – two tablets in the morning for 5 days; medication name and dose not documented; route oral.
  - Spacer device with instructions.
- Allergies:
  - No known drug allergies.
  - Environmental: dust.

Social History:
- University student; was away at university last week and forgot inhalers.
- Tobacco, alcohol, substance use: Not documented.

Family History:
- Father: Asthma.
- Mother: Eczema.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded.
- Functional status (from history): Not short of breath at rest; exertional dyspnea on stairs.

Investigations:
- None performed/recorded.
- Peak flow: Not available.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Acute asthma exacerbation, likely viral-triggered and precipitated by 1-week lapse in controller/reliever inhalers; currently mild-to-moderate by history (no rest dyspnea), but notable history of prior severe exacerbation.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Acute asthma exacerbation – Supported by known asthma, wheeze, chest tightness, recent URI, and lack of inhaler use; limited by absence of objective measures.
  - Post-viral bronchial hyperreactivity – Possible contributor given recent cold and persistent cough; overlap with asthma.
  - Pulmonary embolism/pneumothorax/pneumonia (low likelihood) – Acute onset dyspnea could fit, but no pleuritic chest pain, no rest dyspnea, non-productive cough, and wheeze with known asthma favor asthma; no risk factors noted. 

- Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation
  - Plan:
    - Re-prescribe salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler; PRN use; seek medical attention if needing more often than every 3 hours. Dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Re-prescribe beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler; resume controller use in the morning once recovering. Dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Start oral steroid course: two tablets each morning for 5 days; medication name/dose not documented; counselled on potential side effects (mood changes, elevated blood sugar, rash, nausea, headache) and to read label.
    - Provide spacer and instructions for correct technique.
    - Rest advised; time off from work/activities as needed (self-certification for up to 7 days discussed).
    - Safety-netting: Seek urgent care for worsening shortness of breath, increasing chest tightness/pain, light-headedness, or any deterioration.

- Issue 2: Medication lapse/non-availability
  - Plan:
    - Urgent refills for SABA and ICS and provision of a spacer.
    - Reinforce consistent controller use as instructed; use SABA only as needed.

- Issue 3: Recent viral upper respiratory illness with persistent cough
  - Plan:
    - No specific treatments recorded; monitor as symptoms improve with asthma management.

- General plan items:
  - Prescriptions to be sent promptly (within the hour, per discussion).
  - Patient education materials/instructions included with spacer.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: Vitals, physical examination, objective airflow measure (peak flow/spirometry), smoking/alcohol/substance history, medication doses and frequencies, steroid medication name/dose, formal follow-up plan.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Minor audio dropouts; steroid name and exact dosing not captured.
